title: The molecules of life: carbohydrate, fat, protein
goal: Describe carbohydrates, fats and proteins, where and how much of each is stored in the body, and why the small glycogen store matters so much.

steps.title: Carbohydrate: glucose and glycogen
steps.text:
Carbohydrates are built from sugars. The one that matters most is **glucose**, a sugar with six carbon atoms. Cells can't keep loose glucose in bulk, so they link thousands of glucose units into branched particles of [glycogen](g:glycogen).

Where the body keeps it [[c:carb-stores]]:

| store | amount |
|---|---|
| muscle glycogen | about 400 g |
| liver glycogen | about 80–100 g |
| blood glucose | about 4–5 g |

The two big stores do different jobs. Muscle glycogen fuels the muscle that holds it. Liver glycogen tops up the blood, so the brain and working muscles keep getting glucose [[c:liver-job]]. That is why a long ride on an empty stomach can make your head foggy before your legs fail.

claims.text: The body stores about 400 g of glycogen in muscle and about 80–100 g in the liver, with only 4–5 g of glucose in the blood.

evidence.quote: Carbohydrate is predominantly stored as glycogen in both the liver (approximately 100 g) and muscle (approximately 400 g) with 5 g also circulating in the blood stream as glucose.
The > 80 g of glucose stored as liver glycogen is used to constantly replenish the 4 g of glucose circulating in the blood.

claims.text: Liver glycogen is released as glucose to keep blood glucose steady, which the brain depends on.

evidence.quote: To ensure the brain has an ample supply of glucose, the liver releases glucose into the bloodstream at a rate similar to the uptake of glucose from the blood into tissues, thereby stabilizing blood glucose concentration between 4.0 and 5.5 mmol/L (70–100 mg/dL).

steps.title: Fat: fatty acids and triglycerides
steps.text:
A [fatty acid](g:fatty-acid) is a long chain of carbon atoms. Three fatty acids joined to a small backbone (glycerol) make a [triglyceride](g:triglyceride), the storage form of fat.

Fat is stored in two main places [[c:fat-sources]]:

- [Adipose tissue](g:adipose-tissue) under the skin and around the organs. Even a lean athlete at 7–14% body fat carries more than 125,000 kJ (30,000 kcal) there [[c:adipose-store]].
- **Inside muscle fibres** as small droplets, called [IMTG](g:imtg), mostly in type I fibres right next to the mitochondria that burn them [[c:imtg-place]].

Fat from adipose tissue must be split, carried in the blood and taken up by the muscle before it can be burned; IMTG is already in place.

claims.text: Fat burned in exercise comes from adipose tissue fatty acids, intramuscular triglycerides and dietary fat.

evidence.quote: Lipids as a fuel source for energy supply during submaximal exercise originate from subcutaneous adipose tissue derived fatty acids (FA), intramuscular triacylglycerides (IMTG), cholesterol and dietary fat.

claims.text: A person with 7–14% body fat stores more than 30,000 kcal (about 125,000 kJ) in adipose tissue.

evidence.quote: A person with 7–14% body fat has >30,000 kcal of energy reserves stored in adipose tissue

claims.text: Intramuscular triglyceride sits mainly in type I fibres, close to the mitochondria.

evidence.quote: Intramuscular triacylglyerides are arranged within striated muscle, primarily in type I fibers in close proximity to the mitochondria

steps.title: A small carbohydrate tank, a huge fat tank
steps.text:
[Oxidising](g:oxidation) carbohydrate releases about **17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram**; fat gives more than twice as much, about **37 kJ (9 kcal) per gram** [[c:carb-energy]]. So all the body's glycogen holds roughly 500 g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ ≈ 8,500 kJ (2,000 kcal). The fat store holds over ten times more.

Yet muscle relies on that small tank: glycogen is only about 4% of the body's fuel stores, but it is the main fuel at moderate and higher intensity [[c:glycogen-main]]. Why muscle can't just switch to fat at race pace is about the *rate* of each pathway, which the bioenergetics module covers.

For now, keep the sizes in mind: carbohydrate is the limited, precious store; fat is the almost endless one.

claims.text: Carbohydrate yields about 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram and fat about 37 kJ (9 kcal) per gram.

evidence.quote: The energy values are 17 kJ/g (4.0 kcal/g) for protein, 37 kJ/g (9.0 kcal/g) for fat and 17 kJ/g (4.0 kcal/g) for carbohydrates.
for a 50-kg (110-lb) athlete, 10 g carbohydrate/kg BW/day is the equivalent of 500 g of carbohydrate (2000 kcal).

claims.text: Muscle and liver glycogen are only about 4% of total fuel stores, yet muscle glycogen is the main fuel at moderate and higher intensity.

evidence.quote: Although muscle and liver glycogen represent just 4% of the body's total fuel stores, muscle glycogen is the primary fuel during exercise of moderate or greater intensity.

steps.title: How much energy is in your glycogen, and how long would it last?
steps.problem: A cyclist has 400 g of muscle glycogen and 100 g of liver glycogen. Carbohydrate gives about 17 kJ per gram. (1) How much energy is stored? (2) If her legs used carbohydrate at 2 g·min⁻¹ and could only draw on the 400 g in muscle, how long would that last?
steps: Energy = mass × energy per gram = 500 g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ = 8,500 kJ. Check: 8,500 ÷ 4.184 ≈ 2,000 kcal.
Time = store ÷ rate of use = 400 g ÷ 2 g·min⁻¹ = 200 min, about 3 h 20 min.
That is a ceiling, not a forecast: not all muscle glycogen sits in the working muscles, and fat, blood glucose and food also supply energy.

steps.title: Protein: the body's machinery, not its fuel tank
steps.text:
Proteins are chains of [amino acids](g:amino-acid) (20 kinds), folded into shapes that do work: the filaments that pull, the enzymes that run every reaction, the pumps and transporters in membranes. Muscle holds half or more of the body's protein [[c:muscle-protein]].

There is no protein store kept for fuel. Every gram is doing a job, so burning it means taking machinery apart. In exercise, amino acid oxidation supplies only about **1–5%** of the energy [[c:protein-fuel]]; it rises a bit when glycogen runs low.

This is why protein matters to endurance athletes for repair and adaptation (building more mitochondria and enzymes), not as a race fuel.

claims.text: Skeletal muscle contains 50–75% of all body proteins.

evidence.quote: In humans, skeletal muscle comprises approximately 40% of total body weight and contains 50-75% of all body proteins.

claims.text: Oxidation of protein and amino acids supplies about 1–5% of the total energy cost of exercise.

evidence.quote: oxidation of protein/amino acids during exercise (approximately 1–5% of the total energy cost of exercise)

points: Carbohydrate is stored as glycogen: about 400 g in muscle, 80–100 g in liver, and only 4–5 g as blood glucose.
Fat is stored as triglyceride in adipose tissue (over 125,000 kJ even in lean athletes) and as IMTG droplets beside the mitochondria.
Carbohydrate gives about 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram, fat about 37 kJ (9 kcal); all glycogen holds about 8,500 kJ, a small but vital tank.
Protein is working machinery, not a fuel store; amino acids supply only about 1–5% of exercise energy.

variants.stem: In a lean, well-fed athlete, which store holds the most energy?

options.why: Right: even at 7–14% body fat, adipose tissue holds more than 125,000 kJ, many times the glycogen store.
Muscle glycogen (about 400 g, roughly 7,000 kJ) is the biggest carbohydrate store but small next to fat.
The liver holds only about 80–100 g of glycogen.
The blood carries only 4–5 g of glucose at any time.

variants.stem: A runner at 9% body fat lines up for a marathon. Rank by energy content: which store is the largest?

options.why: Right: more than 125,000 kJ (30,000 kcal), over ten times all the glycogen.
About 400 g, roughly 7,000 kJ: large for carbohydrate, small next to fat.
About 80–100 g, under 2,000 kJ.
Protein isn't a fuel store; it is working machinery and supplies only 1–5% of exercise energy.

variants.stem: Where is most of the body's glycogen stored?

options.why: Right: about 400 g, against about 100 g in the liver.
The liver holds only about 80–100 g; muscle, with far more mass, holds about 400 g.
The blood holds glucose, not glycogen, and only 4–5 g of it.
Adipose tissue stores fat (triglyceride), not glycogen.

variants.stem: Three hours into a long ride without food, a cyclist feels light-headed and can't concentrate. Which store running low best explains this?

options.text: Liver glycogen, which keeps blood glucose up for the brain
options.why: Right: the liver releases glucose to hold blood glucose steady; when it runs low, the brain is short of fuel.

options.text: Muscle glycogen, which muscles share with the brain
options.why: Muscle glycogen fuels the muscle that stores it; the brain relies on blood glucose from the liver.

options.text: Adipose fat, which is the brain's main fuel
options.why: The brain runs mainly on glucose, and fat stores are nowhere near empty after 3 h.

options.text: Muscle protein, which the brain burns when hungry
options.why: Protein supplies only a few % of energy and is not what fails here.

variants.stem: During a long, easy triathlon training ride, some fat burned comes from droplets inside the leg fibres. Where in the fibre are these droplets mostly found?

options.text: In type I fibres, next to the mitochondria
options.why: Right: IMTG sits mainly in type I fibres, close to the mitochondria that oxidise it.

options.text: In type II fibres, next to the SR
options.why: IMTG is mostly in type I fibres, near mitochondria, not near the calcium store.

options.text: Inside the nuclei of the fibre
options.why: Nuclei hold DNA; fat droplets sit in the cytosol near mitochondria.

options.text: Outside the fibre, in the blood vessels
options.why: That describes fat in transport; IMTG is stored inside the fibre itself.

variants.stem: After carbohydrate loading, a cyclist holds 600 g of muscle glycogen and 100 g of liver glycogen. Carbohydrate gives about 17 kJ per gram. How much energy is stored as glycogen?

options.why: Right: (600 + 100) g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ = 11,900 kJ (about 2,840 kcal).
This uses 4 per gram, the kcal factor, and labels the answer kJ: 700 × 4 = 2,800 kcal, not kJ.
This leaves out the liver: 600 × 17. The question asks for all glycogen.
This divides mass by energy per gram (700 ÷ 17). Energy = mass × energy per gram.

variants.stem: After an overnight fast, a runner has 400 g of muscle glycogen and only 40 g of liver glycogen. Carbohydrate gives about 17 kJ per gram. How much energy is stored as glycogen?

options.why: Right: (400 + 40) g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ = 7,480 kJ (about 1,790 kcal).
This uses 4 per gram, the kcal factor, and labels the answer kJ: 440 × 4 = 1,760 kcal.
This leaves out the liver: 400 × 17.
This divides mass by energy per gram (440 ÷ 17). Energy = mass × energy per gram.

variants.solution: Total glycogen = 400 g + 40 g = 440 g. Energy = 440 g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ = 7,480 kJ (7,480 ÷ 4.184 ≈ 1,790 kcal).

variants.stem: A triathlete holds 500 g of muscle glycogen and 80 g of liver glycogen. Carbohydrate gives about 17 kJ per gram. How much energy is stored as glycogen?

options.why: Right: (500 + 80) g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ = 9,860 kJ (about 2,360 kcal).
This uses 4 per gram, the kcal factor, and labels the answer kJ: 580 × 4 = 2,320 kcal.
This leaves out the liver: 500 × 17.
This divides mass by energy per gram (580 ÷ 17). Energy = mass × energy per gram.

variants.solution: Total glycogen = 500 g + 80 g = 580 g. Energy = 580 g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ = 9,860 kJ (9,860 ÷ 4.184 ≈ 2,360 kcal).

variants.stem: A cyclist rides hard enough to use carbohydrate at 3 g·min⁻¹. If only her 450 g of muscle glycogen were available, what is the most it could last?

options.why: Right: 450 g ÷ 3 g·min⁻¹ = 150 min (2 h 30 min).
This multiplies store by rate (450 × 3); the units don't give minutes.
This converts 150 min to hours (2.5) and then labels it minutes.
This divides rate by store (3 ÷ 450). Time = store ÷ rate.

variants.solution: Time = store ÷ rate = 450 g ÷ 3 g·min⁻¹ = 150 min = 2 h 30 min. A ceiling only: fat, blood glucose and food also contribute, and not all glycogen is in the working muscles.

variants.stem: A marathoner uses carbohydrate at 2.5 g·min⁻¹. If only his 400 g of muscle glycogen were available, what is the most it could last?

options.why: Right: 400 g ÷ 2.5 g·min⁻¹ = 160 min (2 h 40 min).
This multiplies store by rate (400 × 2.5).
This converts 160 min to hours (2.7) and then labels it minutes.
This divides rate by store (2.5 ÷ 400). Time = store ÷ rate.

variants.solution: Time = store ÷ rate = 400 g ÷ 2.5 g·min⁻¹ = 160 min = 2 h 40 min. A ceiling only: fat and blood glucose also contribute.

variants.stem: An Ironman athlete on the bike uses carbohydrate at 2 g·min⁻¹. If only her 500 g of muscle glycogen were available, what is the most it could last?

options.why: Right: 500 g ÷ 2 g·min⁻¹ = 250 min (4 h 10 min).
This multiplies store by rate (500 × 2).
This converts 250 min to hours (4.2) and then labels it minutes.
This divides rate by store (2 ÷ 500). Time = store ÷ rate.

variants.solution: Time = store ÷ rate = 500 g ÷ 2 g·min⁻¹ = 250 min ≈ 4 h 10 min. Over a full Ironman, fat and food must cover the rest.

variants.stem: A lean runner carries over 125,000 kJ of fat but only about 8,500 kJ of glycogen. Why is the small glycogen store the one that matters most for marathon pace?

options.text: Muscle relies mainly on glycogen at moderate and higher intensity
options.why: Right: glycogen is only ~4% of fuel stores but the main fuel at moderate or greater intensity, so it runs low first.

options.text: Fat can't be burned during exercise at all
options.why: Fat is burned in all endurance exercise; it just can't cover all the demand at higher intensities.

options.text: Glycogen holds more energy per gram than fat
options.why: The reverse: fat holds about 37 kJ per gram, carbohydrate about 17 kJ. This isn't the reason.

options.text: Fat stores are used up in the first hour
options.why: Fat stores are huge; even a full marathon uses a small fraction of them.

variants.stem: About what share of the energy used in exercise comes from oxidising amino acids?

options.why: Right: protein supplies only a small fraction of exercise energy.
This overstates it several-fold; it may be confused with protein's share of a typical diet.
Carbohydrate and fat supply almost all exercise energy; protein is a minor fuel.
Some amino acids are always oxidised, a little more when glycogen is low.

variants.stem: A cycling forum post says: "On long rides your body burns protein as a main fuel, so eat protein bars instead of carbs." What is the best judgement?

options.text: Wrong: protein supplies only about 1–5% of exercise energy
options.why: Right: carbohydrate and fat supply nearly all the energy; protein matters for repair, not as the main fuel.

options.text: Right: protein is the body's largest fuel store
options.why: Protein isn't a fuel store; each gram is working machinery, and fat is the largest store.

options.text: Right: muscle holds most of the body's protein for fuel
options.why: Muscle does hold most body protein, but as filaments and enzymes, not as a fuel reserve.

options.text: Wrong: the body never oxidises any protein
options.why: A little is always oxidised (1–5%); the post's error is calling it a main fuel.
